claims.claim: Kao and Hockham proposed in 1965 that attenuation in optical fibers was caused by removable impurities rather than fundamental physics, making ultra-pure silica glass the right medium.
claims.episode_span: The answer required glass so free of impurities that a pulse could cross tens of kilometers before fading below detection.
claims.supporting_quote: They proposed that the attenuation in fibers available at the time was caused by impurities that could be removed, rather than by fundamental physical effects such as scattering.

claims.claim: Silica fiber attenuation fell about four orders of magnitude, from ~1000 dB/km in 1965 to ~0.17 dB/km in 2005.
claims.episode_span: driving attenuation from hundreds of decibels per kilometer down to fractions of a decibel
claims.supporting_quote: a four-order-of-magnitude reduction in the attenuation of silica optical fibers over four decades from ~1000 dB/km in 1965 to ~0.17 dB/km in 2005

claims.claim: Fiber preforms are made by vapor deposition in which silicon tetrachloride is reacted with oxygen inside a rotating glass tube.
claims.episode_span: engineers created a preform by reacting silicon tetrachloride and oxygen inside a rotating tube
claims.supporting_quote: the preform starts as a hollow glass tube approximately 40 centimeters (16 in) long, which is placed horizontally and rotated slowly on a lathe . Gases such as silicon tetrachloride (SiCl 4 ) or germanium tetrachloride (GeCl 4 ) are injected with oxygen in the end of the tube.

claims.claim: Long-haul fiber links require repeaters/amplifiers roughly every 70-150 km, consistent with the digest's 80-100 km amplifier spacing.
claims.episode_span: the optical amplifiers still required every eighty to one hundred kilometers
claims.supporting_quote: leading to long-haul fiber connections with repeater distances of 70–150 kilometers (43–93 mi)

claims.claim: The skin effect concentrates alternating current near the surface of a conductor, limiting copper at higher frequencies.
claims.episode_span: The skin effect concentrated current near the conductor surface at higher frequencies
claims.supporting_quote: skin effect is the tendency of an alternating electric current (AC) to become distributed within a conductor such that the current density is largest near the surface of the conductor

claims.claim: In 1966 Charles K. Kao calculated that light could be transmitted over 100 km through a fiber of sufficiently pure glass (versus ~20 m for 1960s fibers), and the first ultrapure fiber was fabricated in 1970 (2009 Nobel Prize in Physics).
claims.episode_span: The answer required glass so free of impurities that a pulse could cross tens of kilometers before fading below detection.
claims.source_title: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2009 - Press release
claims.supporting_quote: In 1966, Charles K. Kao made a discovery that led to a breakthrough in fiber optics. He carefully calculated how to transmit light over long distances via optical glass fibers. With a fiber of purest glass it would be possible to transmit light signals over 100 kilometers, compared to only 20 meters for the fibers available in the 1960s.

claims.claim: In 1970 Corning's Robert Maurer, Donald Keck and Peter Schultz produced the first fiber with loss low enough for telecommunications (about 20 dB/km) by depositing doped silica inside a quartz tube via a vapor-phase (flame-hydrolysis) process.
claims.episode_span: The first concrete move was the development of vapor-phase deposition processes that could reduce transition-metal impurities to parts per billion.
claims.supporting_quote: In 1970 Maurer and his colleagues Donald Keck and Peter C. Schultz designed and produced the first fiber with optical losses low enough for use in telecommunications by a novel process of depositing titania-doped silica inside a quartz tube using a flame-hydrolysis process and sintering, then fusing it to draw into fiber. They demonstrated optical loss as low as 20 dB/km, which for the first time indicated a practical technology.

claims.claim: Semiconductor heterostructure laser diodes (the work of Alferov and Kroemer, 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics) are the light sources that drive fiber-optic communication links.
claims.episode_span: Semiconductor diode lasers, once they reached sufficient reliability and spectral purity, replaced those sources.
claims.source_title: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2000 - Press release
claims.supporting_quote: Zhores I. Alferov and Herbert Kroemer have invented and developed fast opto- and microelectronic components based on layered semiconductor structures, termed semiconductor heterostructures. Fast transistors built using heterostructure technology are used in e.g. radio link satellites and the base stations of mobile telephones. Laser diodes built with the same technology drive the flow of information in the Internet’s fibre-optical cables.
